Frightened

/FRY-tund/ · adjective (past participle of frighten)

Hear It

What It Means

Frightened means filled with fear; afraid, especially in reaction to something specific that just happened.

The frightened kitten shot under the porch at the first crack of thunder and refused to come out.

Worked Example

Frightened by the blaring fire alarm, the first-graders froze in place until their teacher calmly led them to the door.

The children's fear is a direct reaction to one specific event — the alarm going off. Frightened describes the person or animal feeling the fear, and it almost always points back to a particular cause.

How Frightened Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

scared

scared: feeling fear

alarmed

alarmed: suddenly worried that something bad is happening

startled

startled: frightened or shaken by something sudden and unexpected

Antonyms

calm

calm: free of fear or agitation

unafraid

unafraid: feeling no fear

How Strong Is It? — uneasy → frightened → terrified

uneasy vs. frightened

uneasy vs. frightened: Someone uneasy has only a vague sense that something is wrong; someone frightened feels real fear, with a racing heart and the urge to escape.

terrified vs. frightened

terrified vs. frightened: Terrified goes beyond frightened — fear so intense it can freeze you in place or send you into a panic.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — fright

Root — fright: sudden intense fear (Old English fyrhto)

Suffix — -en

Suffix — -en: to make or become (verb-forming, as in shorten, darken)

Suffix — -ed

Suffix — -ed: forms the past participle, used here as an adjective

Put it together

Put it together: Frightened stacks two endings onto the old English word fright ('sudden fear'): -en turns it into the verb frighten ('to make afraid'), and -ed turns that into a description of the one who was made afraid.

Use the root in a new word: frightful

Use the root in a new word: frightful: The abandoned mine had a frightful reputation among the villagers, who refused to go near it after dark.

Word Choice

Neutral / everyday

Watch the direction: frightened describes the one feeling the fear ('the frightened camper'), while frightening describes the thing causing it ('a frightening noise'). You are frightened by a specific event or frightened of something in general — mixing up the -ed and -ing forms is one of the most common usage errors with this word family.
